items.title: Myethos to open pre-orders for Aventurine diorama from Honkai: Star Rail on October 20
items.summary: This week, fans of Aventurine from Honkai: Star Rail and his exclusive Light Cone "An Unfair Fate" will be able to pre-order a new diorama from Myethos.
items.content:
0 Source: Сообщество фанатов Авантюрина на reddit — r/AventurineMainsHSR 19 October 2026, 11:28 Denis Morporkov Translated with AI from the Russian original .

This week, fans of Aventurine from Honkai: Star Rail and his exclusive Light Cone "An Unfair Fate" will be able to pre-order a new diorama from Myethos.

Myethos is once again set to delight fans of the free-to-play role-playing game Honkai: Star Rail. On October 20, 2026, it will open pre-orders for a diorama dedicated to the five-star character Aventurine.

It will be available for 488 Chinese yuan (6053 rubles). The team captured the art of "An Unfair Fate" — a five-star Light Cone of the Preservation Path. The collectible item is 24.2 cm high, 12.6 cm wide, and 20 cm long.

The diorama is expected to be shipped in the third quarter of 2027 (approximately in August).

Aventurine is a top manager in the Strategic Investment Department of the Interastral Peace Corporation and one of the Ten Stonehearts. By nature, he is an incredibly avid gambler, willing to stake everything, including his own life, to achieve profit or a set goal.

Behind the mask of a cynical businessman lies a deep personal drama: his real name is Kakavasha, and he is the sole survivor of the annihilated Augite tribe from the desert planet Sigonia-IV.

Outwardly, Aventurine looks extremely stylish, well-groomed, and luxurious, fully justifying his status as a high-ranking corporate agent. He has short blond hair and unique, mesmerizing eyes with purple-pink irises.

He dresses in an elegant suit with turquoise elements, a fur collar, and an abundance of gold jewelry, watches, and rings. His neck is adorned with a barcode tattoo, reminiscent of his past as a slave, which he hides with a stylish collar, and he often conceals his eyes behind colored sunglasses.

Honkai Star Rail Pity Odds: 0.6% Rate, $361 Cap [2026]
items.summary: Honkai Star Rail pity odds explained: 0.6% base rate, 90-pull hard pity, 50/50 rule, and a worked EV table pricing the guarantee at $195-$361.
items.content:
Short answer: a 5-star character in Honkai Star Rail has a base pull rate of 0.6% on Character Event Warps, with a hard pity guarantee at 90 pulls . Pull a 5-star and you have a 50% chance it’s the featured unit. Lose that coin flip and the game guarantees your very next 5-star is the one you wanted. Do the math on both paths and the expected cost to land a specific featured character lands around 94 pulls , or roughly $195 at current Oneiric Shard pricing. The worst-case scenario, where you lose the 50/50 right at hard pity and then need a full second hard pity to lock in the guarantee, runs to 180 pulls and about $361 in real money. Below is every number behind that math, sourced from HoYoverse’s own in-game probability disclosure and cross-checked against current shop pricing.

How the Warp System Actually Works Base Drop Rates: The Official Numbers Soft Pity vs Hard Pity: Where the Real Odds Shift The 50/50 System and the Guarantee Rule Explained Pity Cost Table: Stellar Jade and Real Cash to Hard Pity Worked Expected-Value Calculation: What a Featured Unit Really Costs Light Cone Warps: Different Rates, Different Pity Five Worked Pull Scenarios With Real Numbers Express Supply Pass and Battle Pass: Do They Change the Math? How Honkai Star Rail’s Odds Compare to Other Gacha Games Is Honkai Star Rail Pay-to-Win or Fair? Myths vs Facts About Honkai Star Rail’s Pity System What the Numbers Mean for Your Wallet Frequently Asked Questions Related Coverage · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.

Honkai Star Rail calls its gacha pulls “Warps,” and they run through four separate banners: the Character Event Warp (limited-time featured characters), the Stellar Warp (the permanent standard pool), the Departure Warp (a cheaper starter banner for new accounts), and the Light Cone Event Warp (limited weapon-equivalent items). Each banner tracks its own pity counter independently, so pulling on the standard banner doesn’t move you closer to a guarantee on the limited character banner.

Every single Warp costs 160 Stellar Jade , whether you buy them one at a time or in the standard 10-pull batch (1,600 Jade). Stellar Jade is earned for free through daily missions, events, and exploration, or purchased as Oneiric Shards, which convert into Stellar Jade at a 1:1 rate the moment you spend real money. That 1:1 conversion is what makes it possible to price a pull in actual dollars instead of just in-game points, and it’s the backbone of every calculation in this piece.

The week's biggest stories in tech, gaming and security, in one email.

HoYoverse publishes exact drop rates inside the in-game probability disclosure on the official Honkai Star Rail site , and the numbers are consistent across every major reference source, including a detailed breakdown from The Loadout’s pity system guide . Here’s what’s officially listed per banner type:

Those base rates only tell part of the story. HoYoverse also publishes a separate, smoothed figure it calls the “average rate including pity,” which sits at roughly 1.6% for 5-star characters on the Character Event and Stellar Warp banners. That average bakes in the fact that your odds climb sharply as you approach hard pity, so it’s the number that actually matters for expected-cost math, not the flat 0.6% base rate.

Hard pity is the only number HoYoverse guarantees in writing: pull 90 times on a Character Event or Stellar Warp banner without a 5-star and the 90th pull is one, no exceptions. What isn’t officially published is the soft pity curve, the point where your odds start climbing above that flat 0.6% baseline before hard pity kicks in.

Independent data-tracking projects that log thousands of real player pulls put the soft pity start somewhere in the low-to-mid 70s for Character Event Warps, with the rate climbing fast each pull after that until it hits 100% at pull 90. Light Cone banners appear to soften a bit earlier, in line with their shorter 80-pull hard cap. Treat those numbers as community estimates, not confirmed HoYoverse data, a distinction Charlie Intel’s pity breakdown also flags for players relying on tracker apps. For a broader breakdown of how soft pity and hard pity interact across gacha games generally, see our soft pity vs hard pity math explainer in our provably fair odds and pity math hub , which walks through the mechanic game-agnostic.

Landing a 5-star on a Character Event Warp doesn’t hand you the featured character outright. There’s a coin flip built into the system: a 50% chance the 5-star you pulled is the banner’s featured character, and a 50% chance it’s a different 5-star drawn from the game’s broader standard pool.

Lose that flip and you’re not starting over. The rule is straightforward: the very next 5-star you pull on that banner type is guaranteed to be the featured character, no matter how many pulls it takes to get there. That guarantee is why the true “worst case” for locking in a specific character isn’t 90 pulls, it’s up to 180, because you could theoretically lose the coin flip on pull 90 and then need a full second 90-pull cycle before the guarantee resolves. Light Cone Event Warps run a similar guarantee-after-loss structure for their featured item, though the exact split between featured and non-featured 5-star Light Cones isn’t spelled out with a public percentage in HoYoverse’s disclosure text the way the character 50/50 is.

Here’s where the odds turn into an actual grocery bill. Oneiric Shards, the currency you buy with real money, are sold in six fixed tiers in the US shop. Buying in bulk gets meaningfully cheaper per shard: the 60-Shard pack runs $0.99 (about $0.0165 per Shard), while the 8,080-Shard pack runs $99.99 (about $0.0124 per Shard), roughly a 25% better rate.

Since a Warp costs 160 Stellar Jade and Oneiric Shards convert 1:1, hitting hard pity on a Character Event Warp (90 pulls) requires 14,400 Jade . Buying that in the most cost-efficient realistic combination of shop packs, one 8,080-pack, one 3,880-pack, one 2,240-pack, and one 330-pack, comes to $184.96 for 14,530 Shards, enough to cover the full 90 pulls with a small surplus.

items.title: Honkai: Nexus Anima Preview: HoYoverse’s Next Big Hit?
items.summary: Our Honkai: Nexus Anima preview explores HoYoverse’s colourful creature collector, covering auto-battles, team-building, and gacha mechanics.
items.content:
The gacha game landscape gets substantially busier every time HoYoverse announces a new title. Genshin Impact propelled the company into the stratosphere, while Honkai: Star Rail and Zenless Zone Zero have since catered to different tastes and helped the developer reach even more corners of the gaming world.

With that in mind, it isn’t surprising to see HoYoverse turn its attention to creature collecting with Honkai: Nexus Anima .

Honkai: Nexus Anima is a little bit of a lot of things. It combines HoYoverse’s familiar taste for dark, twisted storytelling with what might be the company’s most colourful world yet. Almost every corner bursts with detail, helped by the fact that this universe isn’t populated by people alone. It is also home to plenty of adorable monsters.

These creatures, known as Anima, have designs that wouldn’t look out of place in Pokémon. Instead of being divided into conventional elemental categories, however, they have more abstract, mood-driven attributes based on concepts such as Satiation and Dreams. It gives the game’s creatures a distinct identity, even if its inspirations are easy to spot.

You’ll use your Anima in auto-battles, with success largely depending on choosing creatures that work well together and placing them in effective positions. The characters you have access to provide special abilities, while fielding particular combinations of Anima can grant additional bonuses.

The battles themselves aren’t especially complicated, but there appears to be plenty of depth in building an effective team. You’ll want to spend time exploring and catching creatures, both to expand your tactical options and to make your existing Anima stronger.

That progression loop could prove compelling. There is something undeniably satisfying about watching the numbers rise, particularly when each improvement gives you another reason to experiment with your line-up.

The gacha system is split between pulling for characters, who provide new abilities, and pulling for Anima to obtain higher-rarity versions or upgrade those already in your collection. Anima can also be caught in the wild, which makes the monetisation side of the game a little unusual.

The full release will presumably encourage players to pull for the strongest creatures, but being able to find lower-rarity Anima and improve them through play is promising. It may give players the freedom to make their favourites viable by investing time rather than money.

Of course, this is still a gacha game, so monetisation will inevitably be part of the experience. Even if Honkai: Nexus Anima proves relatively welcoming to free-to-play players, it will still be designed to encourage spending.

I enjoy auto-battlers, but their hands-off nature can sometimes make them less engaging over time. Honkai: Nexus Anima’s progression systems should help keep players invested, although much will depend on the variety of challenges available beyond the main campaign.

HoYoverse has become increasingly good at creating entertaining side modes in its recent games, so there is every reason to expect more than a straightforward journey through the story. Whether those additional activities can keep the team-building interesting in the long term remains to be seen.

While I like most of what I’ve seen so far, the story feels a little flimsy. Once again, we play as a protagonist with no memory, a device that is starting to feel like a crutch in games of this kind. It makes delivering exposition easier, but there is something frustrating about beginning another adventure as a character who knows almost nothing about themselves or the world around them.

The villains are more encouraging. They bring a slightly more sinister edge to the otherwise colourful setting, and although the narrative currently feels a little crowded, there is real potential for this to become one of HoYoverse’s darkest stories yet. Given the territory explored by games such as Genshin Impact, that is no small claim.

items.title: Honkai: Nexus Anima is a fun creature collector with an incomprehensible story
items.summary: Honkai: Nexus Anima spins off with creature collecting auto-battling gameplay, making for a fun change of pace, though it doesn't quite fit the story.
items.content:
It’s a big deal whenever HoYoverse launches a new game. While it’s true that a new gacha game pops up almost every day, those same gacha games are almost all lifting references or mechanics wholesale from HoYoverse titles. Genshin Impact put the company on the map and shaped what modern gacha games are, and they’ve followed up that hit with Honkai: Star Rail and Zenless Zone Zero, each one making waves and shaking up the industry just a little bit more. It’s safe to assume that HoYoverse wants that same kind of impact from their next major title, and Honkai: Nexus Anima is certainly shaping up to be a swing in a wild new direction. Unfortunately, it’s a big swing that doesn’t fully connect at this time.

Honkai: Nexus Anima is a pretty unique mix of genres and gameplay hooks. While it’s built around creature collecting and will naturally draw comparisons to Pokémon, you aren’t then taking these monsters into turn-based 1v1 battles. Instead, you use them to dive into Teamfight Tactics-style auto battles between big teams of Anima – the creature name in this world.

I’ve always been curious about these sort of idle-battler games, but never met one that hooked me. Using that formula within the context of an anime gacha game, plus mixing in tons of cute collectable creatures, totally does it for me. At first, the depth of combat doesn’t feel particularly vast. There certainly isn’t a high skill ceiling to this style of battle, even as you start mixing in numerous abilities from your Eidos companions. It’s still satisfying to play, but there is a lack of mechanical difficulty at this stage which would need to ramp up to make for a truly satisfying and absorbing endgame.

Outside of battles, Honkai: Nexus Anima will be pretty familiar to you if you’ve dabbled in HoYoverse games. The tutorial section has you exploring some small interactive maps as your chosen protagonist, feeling pretty similar to the small zones of Zenless Zone Zero or Honkai: Star Rail. When you get into the meat of the game, though, you’re tossed into a pretty rich and wide map that combines the scale of a Genshin Impact region with modern buildings and whimsical fantasy meadows.

The game is beautiful, the map is beautiful, the characters you meet are beautiful…but I don’t quite know how to describe them. There isn’t a very clear genre or style to attach Honkai: Nexus Anima to – the other games in the Honkai line were always melting pots of influence that lean heavily toward sci-fi, and Genshin Impact feels similar with a further lean towards Japanese high-fantasy. Honkai: Nexus Anime is bright and bubbly, but impossible to place in the same way.

The story, meanwhile, is not bright or bubbly, but it’s certainly equally incomprehensible. HoYoverse games have an habit of repeating the same two-hit combo in their stories of giving you an amnesiac protagonist, and tossing you into a multidimensional, intergalactic story full of multiple tiers of entities and shadowy realms and world-ending threats and confusing proper nouns. Honkai: Nexus Anima lays it on as thick as usual, with all the gravitas of a grim sci-fi epic. This is a cutesy creature collector, though. The music is whimsical, and the menus are bubbly, but there’s a disconnect between the vibe the game seems to be cultivating and the vibe the story itself is doing. The dense multi-dimensional gacha stories are an acquired taste to start with, but it’s especially egregious here, and I didn’t feel an investment in or understanding of the world I’m exploring because of it.

And that’s a shame, because it really is so much fun to explore this world. Each Anima you bond with can be summoned outside of battles to wander around with you and bust out their unique abilities. One type can smash through walls, while another can become a hilarious improvised trampoline for you to bounce off. I was pretty addicted to the gameplay loop I found myself in, where I’d spend time exploring the world to find new Anima, then I’d dive into battles to see which ones fit together best in a team. And then, once I found a team I liked, I could set out to keep training and uncapping my favourite Anima to make them as strong as possible.

It’s so much fun to play Honkai: Nexus Anima and it’s take on the creature collecting genre, but from the closed beta test, that gets lost in the bland world and incomprehensible story. Being invested in the characters and the story is my biggest reason for picking up a gacha game, and without that, I already have one foot out the door with Honkai: Nexus Anima. I’m hopeful that, as we head towards the full release, HoYoverse can massage these problems and reel me back in.

items.title: Giving a game another chance
items.summary: Honkai: Star Rail (HSR) celebrated its three-year anniversary on April 26, 2026. I originally started playing back when it first came out, but I stopped not too long after because I didn’t really like it. That was because I had just been playing a different game from HoYoverse, the company that makes HSR, that I...
items.content:
Honkai: Star Rail (HSR) celebrated its three-year anniversary on April 26, 2026. I originally started playing back when it first came out, but I stopped not too long after because I didn’t really like it.

That was because I had just been playing a different game from HoYoverse, the company that makes HSR, that I had to stop playing because of bugs. I also stopped because it was really laggy, but I realized when I started playing again this past December that I had actually originally played on the European server rather than the American one, which was why it was lagging.

Now that I’ve started playing it again for the last four months, I’m wishing I’d never quit.

The game’s story is amazing. With games like HSR where the main character is a self-insert, I tend to fully lean into that role. As such, whenever a major twist happens to a character that the main character has bonded with, I really feel it due to the immersion.

Another thing I like about the story is that HSR keeps you on your toes because it isn’t afraid to kill off playable characters.

I’d played a different game from HoYoverse before HSR, and it wouldn’t dream of killing a playable character, so I went into HSR thinking it’d be the same. That idea went out the window on my second day of playing with the first of many playable character deaths.

Because of that, you end up wanting to make sure you own your favorite characters in case you never see them in the game again. However, since HSR is a gacha game, you’re not guaranteed to get the characters you want when they’re available without spending money.

At least that’s what you’d think, but from my experience, HSR is the easiest gacha game I’ve played when it comes to getting the characters you want without spending money.

I’ve managed to get three characters I’ve wanted along with two of their exclusive items without spending money. That’s because HSR makes it really easy to get the in-game currency for pulling characters. That means if you just want to get a character for the sake of having them, you can.

In fact, I’d say HSR is probably the only gacha game where you don’t have to spend real money. I only spent money on cosmetics, but most cosmetics are free rewards from permanent events.

The only negative thing I have to say about the game is that the newer main quests are fairly long.

The latest finished questline takes 62 hours to complete, and the entire main quest line is currently over 100 hours. Because of that, if you have a busy daily schedule, it could take a while to complete. It is possible to finish in a week, but based on personal experience, I wouldn’t recommend it.

The length aside, I would highly recommend this game, especially since it’s free on PC and you don’t even need a gaming one as I play on my laptop. With the three years of content in the game so far, I can’t wait to see where it goes from here.

items.title: "Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.2 "So Laughed the Masses" will arrive on April 22"
items.summary: The Path of Elation awaits when Version 4.2 'So Laughed the Masses' launches on April 22nd.
items.content:
SINGAPORE, April 10, 2026 — Global interactive entertainment brand HoYoverse announced today that Honkai: Star Rail's new Version 4.2, "So Laughed the Masses," will officially launch on April 22. With the rewards of Phantasmoon Games receiving a massive escalation, more eyes across the universe will converge on Planarcadia, and the intensity of the competition will greatly increase. Embrace the new power of the Path of Elation, and march towards final victory alongside Silver Wolf LV.999, who has completed her ascension, and the observer Evanescia! Click to watch the latest trailer: https://youtu.be/NyM_seY0XKg

Click here to obtain the media kit: https://hoyoverse.box.com/s/u3ej6hdz0s88q3x75qkx8kr5f5fy3ewb Meanwhile, to celebrate the upcoming third anniversary of Honkai: Star Rail, the game has meticulously prepared a series of special events and generous rewards, inviting players to join in on the fun. In Version 4.2, the anniversary-exclusive event "Festive Gifts" will make its return, allowing players to check in and receive a total of 20 pulls. Also returning is another highly anticipated player tradition: on the anniversary day of April 26, Trailblazers can select a blessing card from a companion and receive a special gift of 1,600 Stellar Jades. Not to mention, the third-anniversary birthday surprises are an absolute must-see: the limited 5-star characters Huohuo and Robin will be added to the "Stellar Convergence" Store. As is tradition, Trailblazers can use a freely claimed Golden Companion Spirit to exchange for their companion of choice in the store. Furthermore, in addition to the annual first-time top-up double bonus reset, there's even more content waiting for players to explore, including new arrivals in the Gift of Stardust Store and a new Outfit for Castorice! As the anniversary celebration approaches, participate in the "Aha's Chosen: Spreading Elation Everywhere" online event and leave your message for a chance to win multiple grand prizes, including a "Crown of Aha" Silver Wolf LV.999-themed car. At the same time, global cities such as Tokyo, Seoul, and Los Angeles will progressively launch a series of online and offline celebration activities, including themed parades, street festivities, and brand collaborations. For more details, please visit the official website: https://hoyo.link/GXrf0ZdtR In the Version 4.2 Main Story, the stakes of the Phantasmoon Games become a whole lot more complicated once it's announced that the ultimate reward has received an unprecedented escalation: the victor will become the permanent Aeon of Elation. Caught right in the center of the spotlight, the Trailblazer naturally draws the scrutiny and wariness of every major faction. At that moment, Fulwish — leader of the Research Society of Happy Smiles and a local media mogul — invited all Supplicants to the Fulwish TV headquarters in Seafeld City, a holiday resort renowned for its crisp scenery and idyllic climate. There, Fulwish plans to host a televised debate open to all of arcadia, exploring the burning question: "What kind of future will the Phantasmoon Games bring to this world?" For the Trailblazer, this "public provocation" is undoubtedly an overt scheme that is impossible to refuse. And beneath the surface of the debate lurks a myriad of traps and tricks. Pitted against Fulwish, a master at swaying minds and inciting public opinion, can the Trailblazer navigate every hurdle, gather more Wishpower, and resolve the hidden crisis? Meanwhile, fellow Supplicants Silver Wolf and Pearl have struck a mysterious deal that might just be the key to turning the tide of battle. With the competition heating up, two brand-new 5-star characters Silver Wolf LV.999 and Evanescia will officially join the team, becoming crucial companions to help the Trailblazer turn the tables. First up, a familiar face: Silver Wolf is making her grand entrance with a brand-new look. As a long-time member of the Stellaron Hunters, she needs no introduction. If you had to pick the universe's most hardcore gamer, Silver Wolf takes the crown, hands down. If you treat the vast universe as a game of endless level ups and progress, then "Silver Wolf LV.999" is what happens when she hits level 999 and evolves into a "Godmode Player." This hacker from Punklorde also happens to be the very first Emanator of the Elation from the Phantasmoon Games to step into the spotlight. Silver Wolf LV.999 is a 5-star Imaginary character following the Path of Elation. In combat, she can rack up "Hidden MMR" to activate her exclusive Cartridge and enter the "Godmode Player" state. Once active, Silver Wolf pulls both teammates and enemies alike into her own gaming domain, unlocking a "Reward stage" at the start of her turn. During this "Reward stage," she can use her Cartridge to spawn various in-game items, not only shaking up the combat dynamics but also sharing powerful buffs with teammates to turn the tide together. When "Aha Instant" strikes, Silver Wolf blasts all enemies with a game-crashing laser cannon, dealing massive DMG. On top of that, this hacker from Punklorde has one more trick up her sleeve: when a teammate falls under enemy control, she'll hack into the battlefield — even if she isn't actively in the team — granting allies temporary immunity to control. It's her own special way of keeping the team protected during every battle. Next up is Evanescia. Since the start of the Phantasmoon Games, this mysterious girl has always been watching this game's progress as an observer. In fact, as a "Special Observer," Evanescia has participated in far more than just one iteration of the Phantasmoon Games. Because of this, this multi-playthrough player has already witnessed way too many contestants scheming against one another to fight for Wishpower, and watched countless people repeatedly clash on the heels of Aeonic power. Rather than looking forward to who will become the ultimate champion of the Phantasmoon Games, she pays much more attention to the performance of her favored "protagonist": the Trailblazer. And in the new story, more secrets regarding Evanescia's true identity will also gradually reach a final revelation. Evanescia is a 5-star Physical character following the Path of Elation. In combat, Evanescia can continuously accumulate "Certified Banger" through various means: whether she regenerates Energy, teammates Charge her, or the "Certified Banger" on her teammates changes, she continues to gain "Certified Banger." Whenever Evanescia gains "Certified Banger," she will simultaneously regenerate Energy, allowing her to maintain her DMG rhythm. As "Certified Banger" continues to accumulate, Evanescia's DMG will also gradually increase. Whenever it reaches a certain number of points, it will additionally trigger an attack from "Master Fox," dealing DMG to all enemies and regenerating Energy for Evanescia. Her Elation Skill can also attack all enemies. While delivering a stylish performance, it will further increase the team's overall DMG. In addition to the two highly anticipated new characters, the Trailblazer on the Path of Elation will also join the team in Version 4.2. As the Elation Trailblazer's brand-new weapon, the glow stick features a rich variety of uses. When using their Skill, the glow stick transforms into a lightblade as the Trailblazer deals DMG to all enemies and gains "Certified Banger". Not only that, the glow stick can also turn into nunchucks, unleashing a spectacular flurry of attacks on surrounding enemies and dealing multiple instances of DMG. Beyond that, it can also be used to hype up teammates. When using their Ultimate, the Trailblazer can select a teammate to cheer for. This allows the chosen teammate to gain "Certified Banger" while immediately using their Elation Skill, paving the way for an even more lively combat experience! Additionally, a special Warp event will kick off in the first half of Version 4.2. Limited 5-star characters The Dahlia, Castorice, and Firefly will be getting a rerun. Meanwhile, in the Warp event for the second half, limited 5-star characters Tribbie, Sunday, and Feixiao will also have their reruns. On top of that, four existing characters — Firefly, Huohuo, Seele, and Welt — will all be receiving buffs, continuing to provide indispensable help for players on their trailblazing expedition. Finally, right in time for the 3rd Anniversary of Honkai: Star Rail, a host of exciting events will be arriving alongside the grand festivities. In Version 4.2, the brand-new event "Cosmic Data Roaming" will officially go live, allowing Trailblazers to build a top-tier streamer career by broadcasting their sleekest combat moments. Following the version update, Currency Wars will also receive a massive expansion, offering Trailblazers more diverse gameplay options. Meanwhile, the Cosmicon Collective is bringing the heat with its Version 2.0 update, "Cosmicon, Roll On Again!," introducing not only new decks and dice, but also a brand-new team challenge gameplay mode. In addition, exciting events and features like "Express Renovation Escapade" and "Relic Recon" will also be rolling out to help Trailblazers fully enjoy the anniversary fun. At the end of this Special Program, the original animation project co-produced by HoYoverse and MAPPA premiered its concept trailer, "Death in the Afternoon." Please look forward to the continuing cosmic adventures! Honkai: Star Rail is now available on PC, iOS, Android, Epic Games Store, and PS5, and has exceeded 150 million total downloads across all platforms. In 2023, the game won Apple's App Store iPhone Game of the Year, Google Play's Best Game, and BEST MOBILE GAME by The Game Awards. In 2024, it received the Golden Joystick Awards Still Playing Award (Mobile) and PlayStation® Partner Awards 2024 PARTNER AWARD among other honors. The game has been rated Teen by the ESRB and is also classified as PEGI 12. If you wish to learn more details, please visit https://hsr.hoyoverse.com or follow @HonkaiStarRail on Twitter (X), Instagram, and Facebook. About Honkai: Star Rail Honkai: Star Rail is a space fantasy RPG title with a journey through immense worlds of the unknown. The player takes on the role of "Trailblazer," a courageous individual implanted with a powerful artifact, Stellaron, and bearing the determination to unravel the mysteries surrounding the fabled "Cancer of All Worlds" and Aeons. The game features fantasy elements with myths and legends integrated into the space sci-fi story. Combined with the intuitive turn-based combat system, diverse and distinctive companions, and immersive storylines that together compose an interstellar melody filled with captivating worlds, each brimming with unique cultures, awe-inspiring landscapes, and mythical wonders to explore. About HoYoverse HoYoverse is committed to providing immersive virtual world experiences to players around the world. We have brought fans popular games including Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, Honkai Impact 3rd, Tears of Themis, and Zenless Zone Zero, as well as a wide range of entertainment content. Community is at the heart of everything we do. We are devoted to engaging fans and fostering an enthusiastic and inclusive global community that provides access and encouragement for people to share their passion for ACG (Animation, Comics, and Games) through their own creativity and skills. Pushing the boundaries of imagination, we consistently explore cutting-edge game development technologies, and have accumulated leading technical capabilities in cel shading, cloud gaming, and other fields. In the future, we will continue to expand our content production, technology research, and publishing duties through operations in offices in Singapore, Montreal, Los Angeles, Tokyo, Seoul, and other areas. items.title: Honkai: Star Rail 4.0 impressions
items.content:
I'll admit, I recently burned out on Honkai: Star Rail. Upon hearing the news that 3.8 would be the lengthiest patch yet and with content more sparse than ever before, I decided to take a break for the first time since I started playing all the way back in 1.0. The entire Amphoreus saga left me feeling drained; I thoroughly enjoyed 3.0-3.4 as excellent set-up chapters, but felt lost as the plot became a labyrinth of hidden motivations, layered twists, hours of exposition, and endless proper nouns. When looking at the story as a whole, I love the characters (Aglaea and Anaxa in particular) and the rich history of the world within the Scepter, but the later patches often felt like studying for a needlessly convoluted test. I understood the gist of what was happening, but I won't lie to you and say I could describe to you in detail what Cyrene's deal is or how Evernight fits into everything.

All that's to say: I was looking forward to the Astral Express crew taking a well-earned vacation to Planarcadia, the planet of Elation. Despite two of the game's four current versions ostensibly beginning with Akivili's disciples deciding that they need a break from the backbreaking work of saving the universe, neither has resulted in our trailblazers seeing much downtime. Unlike previous excursions, it's all hands on deck: everyone gets off at this stop (save for Black Swan's incredibly hasty and unfortunate exit prior to departure). It's fun to see the entire main cast get involved, none more welcome than Himeko — up until now, the only character trait I could've told you about her was that she's terrible at making coffee. Getting some elaboration on her backstory and giving her a personality outside of "Express mom" is long overdue.

The Trailblazer and March 7th begin their Planarcadian getaway with a suitably devious greeting by none other than our old pal Sparkle. We're given a tour of the vibrant, totally-not-Japanese-inspired streets, crawling with humans living in tentative harmony with totally-not-Penaconian-memetic-entities known as imagenae. Here, we catch a glimpse of what I hope will become one of Planarcadia's core themes: gentrification and the plight of capitalism, with a side of anti-imperialism (all perpetrated by the IPC, of course). It's bold, though, and I worry that future patches will keep these criticisms in the background rather than highlight them as Planarcadia's core issues. I would love so much for little nuggets of lore to be elaborated upon, ones that suggest a more serious political history than Aha would have you believe: what did the imagenae do before the IPC forced them to integrate into society? Were they not allowed to work at all? Were they marginalized and seen as second-class citizens? Is the Department of Aberration Defense an inherently evil organization left to determine on their own which imagenae deserve their continued existence and which do not? Is Kuchiba so hot that it doesn't even matter?

This brings us to the Synwish Syndicate, a gang formerly designed to be a respite for imagenae that feel rejected elsewhere, now, due to IPC intervention, a gang that largely exists to enable monetary gain by questionable means. Here at the syndicate's headquarters, the plot quickly begins to balloon into what feels like a collection of introductions for what's to come. We have Pearl's cold and calculating grip on the planet, Himeko and her confounding family history, the potential return of the Herald of Death, the Stellaron Hunters' unknown involvement in the Phantasmoon Games, Sunday's inadvertent entry into the Games, Evanescia's whole...thing, and Yao Guang's bottomless supply of divinations. What's most shocking is that the patch still manages to pull off a fun (if bloated) self-contained story, adding layers to one of HSR's most inscrutable characters and ending things with one of the game's best low-stakes twists.

I'm no Xianzhou Arbiter-General, but I can pretty easily peer into the future and divine a prophecy for Honkai: Star Rail: each new patch will introduce and/or discuss at length a new prophecy that cryptically divulges the fate of a character and/or planet and/or simulation masquerading as a planet. It's hard to pinpoint the moment a theme becomes a crutch, but I think HSR passed that moment long ago. In this patch, we have not one, not two, but three central characters that are defined by their relationship with prophecy and prediction — Yao Guang, Pearl, and the perennial mystery that is Elio and his script. So many in-game conversations devolve into the interpretation of prophecy, and frankly, it's becoming exhausting. We went through an entire version in which each Chrysos Heir had a poetically vague predetermined fate, and before that (and in 3.8's ret-con-y confusion) we had Sparkle's ambiguous "three deaths" for Firefly.

If this were a wholesale replacement for well-executed foreshadowing, we would have a far bigger issue. It's obvious, though, that the writing team knows how to tell a story sans-prophecy, evident in Sparkle's character-driven narrative in this very patch. Sparxie being the "true" Sparkle (as much as old Sparkle is also the "true" Sparkle) is teased so perfectly; the reveal is obvious in retrospect while being difficult to predict with the given information. It's consistently groan-inducing to see this writing cheat code being used ad nauseam within a story that could function better without it. I hope I'll be proven wrong and the game will subvert the words of its murky prophets, leaving me with egg on my face come the conclusion of this leg of the Express' journey.

4.0 is a promising new beginning, and has at the very least brought me back in terms of its story. Though there is an abundance of new proper nouns to memorize and a bevy of new and returning cast members to keep track of, the patch still takes on a welcome return to simplicity and levity (save for the shocking tonal shift right at the end, RIP the Synwish Syndicate Feb. 2026 - Feb. 2026). As long as things don't get too bogged down in extensive metaphors and tiresome exposition, I'm hopeful that Planarcadia can become the most focused version of HSR we've seen so far.
